These are long-term employees, so it's worth thinking concretely about what transition looks like for them — whether retraining for other roles in your facility is realistic, what severance or placement support you can offer, and how much lead time you can give them. How you handle this will also be noticed by the rest of your workforce, which affects morale and retention more broadly. Second, the actual cost picture. Automation capital costs, installation, maintenance contracts, and retraining or hiring for oversight roles all belong in the calculation alongside the per-unit savings. Third, operational risk. Automated systems have their own failure modes, and you'll want redundancy planning in place. Fourth, timeline. A phased rollout can reduce both operational and workforce disruption risks at the same time. None of this means the decision is wrong — but the people dimension in particular is worth planning around carefully rather than treating as a secondary detail.

Set that against the 12% per-unit savings over a realistic payback horizon, typically three to seven years for this type of capital investment. You should also assess output volume assumptions — whether the 12% figure holds across your actual production range and not just at optimal throughput. On the operational side, look at mean time between failures for the specific equipment, vendor support terms, and parts availability. Finally, check whether the automation affects any compliance certifications or quality audit requirements for your product line, since recertification costs and timelines can affect the payback schedule.
